families.name: ID-Based Collaborative Filtering
families.definition: Recommender systems that rely on unique identifiers (IDs) for users and items to model collaborative signals from interaction history.

properties.text: These models have dominated the recommender systems literature for over a decade and are considered state-of-the-art for many tasks.
They effectively capture collaborative filtering signals from user-item interactions.
ID embeddings can be interpreted as subtle features of content and structure, providing value beyond simple identifiers.
Randomly-hashed item IDs are ubiquitously used in recommendation models.

limitations.text: ID-based models struggle with the cold-start problem for new users or items without interaction history.
Learned representations from random hashing prevent generalization across similar items, causing issues with long-tail and unseen items.
They fail to comprehend the essence of raw item contents across diverse modalities such as text, image, audio, and video.
Inconsistent ID mappings hinder model transferability across different recommendation domains.

families.name: Multimodal Content-Based Recommendation
families.definition: Methods that incorporate raw multimedia content features (visual, textual, acoustic) to enhance item and user representations in recommendation models.

properties.text: These systems amalgamate multimodal information into collaborative filtering frameworks to provide more accurate and interpretable recommendations.
Multimodal features mitigate cold-start issues and improve generalization compared to ID-only models.
Models can leverage pre-trained encoders like Vision Transformers and BERT to extract rich semantic features from raw data.
Multimodal approaches allow for the modeling of fine-grained user interests and visual impressions that influence click decisions.

limitations.text: Introducing multimodal encoders with large parameter counts can cause overfitting due to high-dimensional features.
There is often a discrepancy between training tasks and model parameters when using pre-extracted content features.
Multimodal content often contains noise irrelevant to user preference, such as background layouts or semantic-free words.
End-to-end training of multimodal models is computationally costly and challenging to optimize in industrial scenarios.

families.name: Generative Recommendation
families.definition: Frameworks that frame candidate item retrieval or recommendation as an autoregressive sequence generation problem, often using language models.

properties.text: Generative retrieval treats recommendation as a sequence generation task, allowing for flexible handling of various recommendation tasks.
Models like P5 unify different recommendation tasks into a text-to-text paradigm, facilitating knowledge transfer between tasks.
Generative methods can integrate behavioral and semantic information to address the limitations of focusing solely on one aspect.
Large Language Models (LLMs) serve as backbones for these systems, leveraging their reasoning and generation capabilities.

limitations.text: Existing generative methods often neglect the complementary nature of behavioral and semantic information, resulting in limited effectiveness.
There is a significant semantic gap between LLMs and recommender systems because items are indexed by discrete IDs outside the LLM's vocabulary.
Controlling the dialogue flow in LLM-based conversational recommenders to ensure target-oriented recommendations is imperative but difficult.
Simply prompting LLMs for conversational recommendation often fails to effectively model user preferences from feedback.

families.name: Pre-trained Multimodal Foundation Models
families.definition: Large-scale models pre-trained on diverse multimodal data to learn universal representations that can be transferred to various recommendation tasks.

properties.text: These models aim to unify different modalities (vision, language, audio) into a shared semantic space for understanding and generation.
Pre-training on broad-ranging data allows for task-agnostic and unified machine learning systems that break out of task-specific restrictions.
Foundation models can leverage recent large-scale vision-language models to extend zero-shot capabilities to new modalities.
Instance-centric pretraining paradigms are designed to handle the differences between natural and product images in e-commerce.

limitations.text: Directly applying general domain pretraining frameworks to e-commerce is sub-optimal due to significant differences in image distributions.
Training with diverse modalities is challenging and requires specific architectural improvements to stabilize the process.
There is a lack of widely-recognized benchmarking standards for evaluating these large-scale multimodal recommendation models.
The high computational cost of training and serving these large models poses challenges for real-time industrial applications.

families.name: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)
families.definition: Techniques that adapt large pre-trained models to downstream recommendation tasks by training only a small subset of parameters.

properties.text: Methods like LoRA and adapters add only a few trainable parameters per task, allowing for compact and extensible models.
PEFT enables parameter-efficient transfer learning for recommender systems, particularly for adapting pre-trained modality encoders.
These techniques allow new tasks to be added without revisiting previous ones, yielding a high degree of parameter sharing.
Prompt tuning and prefix tuning optimize continuous task-specific vectors while keeping the language model parameters frozen.

limitations.text: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models is parameter-inefficient if a full copy of the model is required for every task.
Existing techniques for combining separate LoRAs for joint generation of styles and subjects often compromise subject or style fidelity.
The effectiveness of adapter-based learning for transferable recommendation systems requires further empirical study and practical insight.

families.name: Conversational Recommender Systems
families.definition: Systems that recommend items through a dialogue interface, utilizing LLMs to manage sub-tasks like preference elicitation and explanation.

properties.text: LLMs have the potential to improve CRS performance by conducting fluent, multi-turn conversations with users.
These systems aim to control the dialogue flow to successfully recommend appropriate items rather than engaging in aimless chit-chat.
User feedback in CRS can assist the system in better modeling user preferences, which is often ignored in existing studies.
Neuro-symbolic reasoning frameworks can be used to provide interpretable reasoning chains for task-oriented dialogues.

limitations.text: It is imperative to control the dialogue flow in LLMs to ensure the system achieves its recommendation target.
Existing studies often ignore the utility of user feedback in refining user preference models during conversation.
Developing effective CRSs involves challenges in managing multiple sub-tasks and generating correct responses that interact with users.

families.name: Explainable and Personalized Generation
families.definition: Methods that generate natural language explanations or personalized content (like headlines) to justify recommendations and enhance user trust.

properties.text: Providing user-understandable explanations helps users understand recommended items and increases system ease of use.
Personalized headline generation incorporates reader preferences to create irresistible reading invitations.
These systems can utilize distant supervision from user click behaviors to learn preference representations.
Human-AI co-creation methods, such as guiding or selecting model outputs, add benefit to the generation process with low cost.

limitations.text: Previous works mostly adopted recurrent neural networks, leaving potentially more effective pre-trained Transformer models under-exploited.
User and item IDs are in a different semantic space than words, making it difficult for pre-trained models to generate explanations directly.
LLMs alone can generate satisfactory headlines, but human control is often needed to fix undesirable model outputs.
Bridging the semantic gap between Large Language Models and recommender systems, where items are indexed by discrete IDs outside the LLM's vocabulary.
Developing a widely-recognized benchmarking standard for recommender systems to address the lack of consistent experimental settings and reproducibility.
Efficiently integrating multimodal encoders into recommendation models without causing overfitting or incurring prohibitive computational costs in industrial scenarios.
Resolving the discrepancy between training and testing signals in cold-start multimedia recommendation, where cold items only exist in testing data.
Creating a universal model that can effectively harness heterogeneous resources and respond to a wide range of personalized needs across different domains.
Improving the interpretability of multimodal recommendation models, which currently represent users and items using entangled numerical vectors.
Addressing the challenge of modality forgetting in two-stage approaches, where the sequential objective overshadows modality representation.
Developing methods to reliably combine separate LoRAs for joint generation of learned styles and subjects without compromising fidelity.
